METHODS: Here, we examined data from 108,182 individuals of European-like ancestry and 13,229 African-like ancestry across two…
papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Current psychiatric diagnoses lack biological grounding. Using transdiagnostic psychiatric dimensions derived through data-driven genetic studies with large-scale clinical health records of multiple physiological and clinical outcomes, we can gain new insights into biological similarity and differences between such dimensions, informing nosological discourse. METHODS: Here, we examined data from 108,182 individuals of European-like ancestry and 13,229 African-like ancestry across two healthcare biobanks. Genetic liabilities of individuals were estimated as polygenic scores for five first-order psychopathology factors (compulsive, thought, neurodevelopmental, substance use, internalizing disorders) and one second-order factor (hierarchical/p-factor). Phenome-wide and laboratory-wide association scans encompassed 1,520 medical phenotypes and 123 laboratory metrics, meta-analyzed across sites. People with lived experience were involved in the design, preparation, interpretation and reporting of this work. OUTCOMES: We observed robust associations with up to 143 conditions (14 disease categories) for first- order factors and 221 conditions (15 categories) for the hierarchical factor (OR=0.75-1.94). Circulatory, digestive, and respiratory diseases were linked to neurodevelopmental, internalizing, and substance use liabilities. Metabolic conditions were negatively associated with thought and compulsive liabilities but positively associated with the remaining three factors. Laboratory results, particularly lipid and glucose metabolism markers, supported these differential findings. Immune markers also showed differential associations, with C- reactive protein and Complement C4 specifically linked to neurodevelopmental and thought factors, respectively. Similar trends emerged in the smaller African-like ancestry sample. INTERPRETATION: Overall, these findings support ongoing efforts to define biologically informed subtypes in psychiatry, such as immuno-metabolic profiles, which can facilitate patient stratification in clinical trials and support transdiagnostic precision psychiatry approaches. FUNDING: The work was supported by funding from the participating institutions. BF's and NRM's contributions were supported by the European Community's Horizon 2020 Programme (H2020/2014-2020) under grant agreement No. 847879 (PRIME). NRM was also supported by the Netherlands Organisation for Scientific Research (NWO) Innovation Programme (Vidi grant No. 09150172410043). Research reported in this publication was also supported by the National Institute of Mental Health of the National Institutes of Health under Award Number R01MH124851. The content is solely the responsibility of the authors and does not necessarily represent the official views of the funders. EVIDENCE BEFORE THIS STUDY: We searched PubMed from database inception to October 13, 2026, without date or language restrictions, using combinations of the terms "transdiagnostic", "cross-disorder", "genomic SEM", "polygenic score", "polygenic risk", "phenome-wide", "PheWAS", "laboratory", and "somatic". We considered original human genetic studies examining transdiagnostic psychiatric genetic liability and its associations with medical or laboratory phenotypes, excluding studies without relevant psychiatric genetic analyses. Previous studies demonstrated shared genetic liability across psychiatric disorders and phenome-wide associations of cross-disorder polygenic scores, although evidence was limited by ancestry representation, sample selection, and phenotypic ascertainment. Studies jointly examining multiple transdiagnostic psychiatric genetic dimensions across medical diagnoses and laboratory biomarkers remain limited. ADDED VALUE OF THIS STUDY: Using EHR-linked data from 121,411 individuals across two US biobanks, we examined six genetically defined transdiagnostic psychiatric factors in relation to 1,520 medical phenotypes and 123 laboratory measures. We identified shared and distinct associations across psychiatric dimensions, particularly involving metabolic, immune, and cardiovascular systems. Findings showed broadly concordant directions of association across genetically inferred ancestry groups, although statistical power was limited in the smaller African-like ancestry cohort. IMPLICATIONS OF ALL THE AVAILABLE EVIDENCE: Our findings highlight the value of transdiagnostic genetic approaches for understanding shared and distinct physiological correlates of psychiatric liability beyond conventional diagnostic boundaries. These associations may inform future research into biologically informed psychiatric stratification and the integration of physical health considerations into psychiatric care, although their clinical utility requires further evaluation.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Methylphenidate is a first-line pharmacological treatment for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in children and adolescents. However, approximately one-third of patients experience inadequate symptom improvement or intolerable adverse effects, and clinicians currently lack biomarkers to guide prescribing decisions. METHODS: The pharmacogenomics of stimulant treatment response study is an open-label clinical trial designed to identify genomic profiles associated with methylphenidate treatment response and tolerability in youth with ADHD. A total of 400 Canadian youth aged 6-24 years who are initiating long-acting methylphenidate treatment are eligible. Participants will provide saliva samples for genome-wide genotyping and complete weekly clinical assessments over 4 weeks, including the Strengths and Weaknesses of ADHD Symptoms and Normal Behaviors Rating Scale, Canadian ADHD Resource Alliance Side Effect Form, neurocognitive tasks, and quality-of-life measures. Blood microsamples will be collected at week 4 for methylphenidate and ritalinic acid concentration determination. Primary analyses will examine associations between genomic profiles, including candidate gene variants, genome-wide significant loci, and polygenic scores for psychiatric disorders and treatment outcomes. Secondary analyses will explore pharmacokinetic correlates of response. DISCUSSION: At the time of writing, 126 participants have been enrolled, of whom 110 have completed the trial protocol. This trial will establish a comprehensive pharmacogenomics research platform to advance precision prescribing of methylphenidate.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is a causal risk factor for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Guidelines recommend reducing saturated fat intake to lower LDL-C, but dietary effects are heterogeneous. OBJECTIVES: We examined whether genetic propensity for higher LDL-C modifies the association of saturated fat intake with LDL-C and incident ASCVD. METHODS: Among 20,940 genotyped Women's Health Initiative participants, we examined saturated fat intake from food frequency questionnaires and a polygenic score for LDL-C (PGSLDL). The primary outcome was LDL-C. The secondary outcome was incident ASCVD. Associations were assessed using multivariable linear and Cox regressions. Effect modification was evaluated using interaction terms and restricted cubic splines. Models included demographic, lifestyle, clinical, and genetic covariates. RESULTS: The association between saturated fat intake and LDL-C was modified by PGSLDL (P interaction for LDL-C = 0.01). Spline analysis revealed a nonlinear interaction, with increasing effect sizes across the upper end of the PGSLDL distribution. Among 16,835 participants without prevalent ASCVD, 1,582 experienced incident ASCVD (median follow-up: 10 years [Q1, Q3: 9.4, 10.0]). A 5% isocaloric increase in saturated fat intake was associated with a higher ASCVD risk among individuals in the top quartile of PGSLDL (HR: 1.26; 95% CI: 1.08-1.47), but no association was observed among those in the bottom 3 quartiles (HR: 1.00; 95% CI: 0.89-1.12); P interaction for ASCVD = 0.006. CONCLUSIONS: The association between saturated fat intake and LDL-C and subsequent ASCVD risk may be stronger for individuals with a genetic propensity towards high LDL-C.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Polygenic risk scores (PRSs), which aggregate the effects of thousands of single-nucleotide variants, can identify individuals at increased genetic risk of common complex diseases. While attracting growing interest for risk-stratified screening and prevention, PRS is not a diagnostic tool, placing responsibility on healthcare providers to interpret results and guide patients in preventive and screening decisions. Although PRS information can support patients, it may also pose a psychological burden. METHODS: In this study, we conducted the first cross-sectional survey of PRS perceptions in the Belgian (Walloon) healthcare context, assessing patients' views in a large cohort (N = 692) alongside specialist physicians' (SPs; N = 52) perspectives on clinical use. The survey evaluated attitudes toward PRS-guided prevention and screening in cancer and noncancer scenarios, as well as perceptions of communication needs and implementation challenges. Descriptive and comparative analyses were used to assess differences between groups and scenarios. RESULTS: Patients more strongly supported preventive actions in cancer-related scenarios than in noncancer conditions (all FDR-adjusted p-value < 1e-4). In both contexts, they favored earlier and more frequent screening and lifestyle modifications while remaining cautious about preventive pharmacotherapy and prophylactic surgery. Neither patients nor SPs supported reduced screening in the low-PRS groups (all median scores ≤ 50 on a 0-100 scale), and both highlighted concerns about psychological burden and potential discrimination. SPs reported limited time to communicate complex risk information, whereas most patients preferred explanations from a genetics specialist or their attending physician, emphasizing expertise and trust. Individual factors, including age, sex, and family history, further influenced perceptions and willingness to act on PRS-guided interventions. CONCLUSIONS: These findings indicate the need for context-specific implementation strategies and support a model in which a single consultation with a genetics specialist provides a clear interpretation of PRS results, followed by the management of preventive actions by the patient's primary care physician.

papers.abstract_full: OBJECTIVE: To explore whether the excess risk of type 2 diabetes (T2D) attributable to genetic predisposition could be mitigated by controlling modifiable risk factors and whether this mitigation is attenuated in individuals with prediabetes. METHODS: We included 382,313 participants from the UK Biobank for T2D analyses. The main exposure was the number of optimally controlled risk factors including non-smoker, high level of physical activity, healthy diet, healthy sleep, low BMI, and non-hypertension. Genetic risk groups were defined as low and high categories based on a median of the T2D polygenic risk score. Cox proportional hazard models were employed to explore the associations of joint risk factor control with T2D. RESULTS: During a median of 13.5 years of follow-up, 9210 incident T2D cases were identified in the high genetic risk group. Among individuals with high genetic risk, those who achieved control of all six risk factors had a lower incidence of T2D than those with low genetic risk (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.79, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.68, 0.92). However, even with all six risk factors were controlled, participants with prediabetes still had a higher risk of developing T2D, compared with those who had low genetic risk and normal glucose levels. CONCLUSION: Our results indicated that optimal risk factor control may mitigate the genetic-related excess risk of T2D, but it cannot fully mitigate the prediabetes-related risk of T2D.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Prediabetes is a heterogeneous condition, with individuals exhibiting varying risks of progression to type 2 diabetes (T2D). We applied data-driven clustering to metabolic variables to identify prediabetes subgroups, evaluated their progression risks, and evaluated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs)-cluster interactions. METHODS: Among 1,016 individuals with prediabetes, k‑prototypes clustering was applied to age, sex, BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, lipid parameters, and HbA1c to derive phenotypic clusters. Incident T2D risk was compared across clusters using Cox proportional‑hazards regression. Interactions between four T2D risk variants (THADA, CDKN2B, SLC30A8, VPS26A) and cluster membership were tested. Cluster‑specific genetic risk was quantified using a polygenic risk score (PRS). RESULTS: Four prediabetes sub-phenotypes were identified: low-risk prediabetes (LORPD), characterized by younger, predominantly female individuals with near-normal BMI and lipid profiles; mild hyperglycemia prediabetes (MIHPD), characterized by modest hyperglycemia with otherwise favorable metabolic characteristics; mild obesity-related prediabetes (MORPD), characterized by obesity-related metabolic abnormalities; and metabolic syndrome prediabetes (MESPD), the most severe group with the highest BMI, waist circumference, blood pressure, and the most adverse lipid profile. Progression to T2D varied markedly by cluster: MESPD cluster had the highest incidence (58.1 per 1,000 person-years) and roughly 24-fold (95% CI 12.88-45.68) compared to controls. In contrast, the LORPD cluster had the lowest progression risk, at 3.35-fold (95% CI 1.15-9.80). The MIHPD (HR 12.88; 95% CI 7.06-23.50) and MORPD (HR 16.26; 95% CI 9.91-26.70) cluster showed intermediate rates of progression to T2D. Significant SNP-cluster interactions were detected. In MESPD, THADA rs7578597 T, CDKN2B rs7018475 G, and VPS26A rs1802295 T increased T2D hazard (HRs 6.77, 4.06, 4.98); in MORPD, SLC30A8 rs13266634 T was associated (HR 3.25). PRS were used to refine risk stratification, with the MESPD cluster showing a significant genetic predisposition to T2D. PRS further improved T2D risk prediction within the LORPD cluster. CONCLUSIONS: These results indicate that although our clusters were delineated solely by clinical phenotype, integrating genetic-cluster interaction data can substantively enhance preventive strategies. Moreover, these findings support precision prevention by tailoring monitoring and interventions to individuals' combined phenotypic and genetic risk profiles.

papers.abstract_full: The excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) imbalance theory suggests that excitatory and inhibitory alterations underlies autism characteristics. However, genetic underpinnings of this imbalance and its impact on brain function and behavior remains unclear. We explored causal links between glutamate and GABA gene-set polygenic scores (PGS) for autism and core autism characteristics, putting particular attention on the restricted- and repetitive behaviors (RRBs) domain by including functional activity (fMRI) during inhibitory control (in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and striatum). Causal links between genes, brain and behavior was evaluated using Bayesian Constraint-based Causal Discovery (BCCD) algorithms, to build causal models of these relationships in a discovery sample (LEAP cohort: autistic = 343, neurotypical = 253) and two generalization cohorts with partially overlapping measures (TACTICS cohort: autistic = 60, neurotypical = 100, Simon Simplex Collection: autistic = 2756). In the discovery sample, we found a causal link between glutamate PGS and core clinical characteristics of autism, particularly the communication domain (Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised) in autistic participants, with 95% reliability. We did not find links between functional activity during inhibitory control and other measures. For one generalization cohort, we further report on the impact of 1H-MRS measures of glutamate, identifying a causal link between GABA autism PGS on ACC glutamate concentrations. Not all links were identified in the generalization cohorts, which may be due to clinical and genetic differences between the cohorts. While our results reinforce the previously found association between glutamate genes and core clinical autism behaviors, task-based functional activity may not be causally related to RRBs.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Salvage stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) for selected patients with recurrent IDH-wildtype glioblastoma (rGB) offers survival benefit, but optimal dosing remains undefined. We evaluated safety, efficacy, and dose-response relationships of single fraction SRS for rGB. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective multicenter study of 271 consecutive patients with rGB treated with single-fraction SRS at first recurrence (2007-2025). Primary outcome was post-recurrence survival (PRS); secondary outcomes included overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS). Multivariable Cox regression, propensity score matching (PSM), and recursive partitioning analysis (RPA) were used to identify prognostic factors. RESULTS: Median age was 61 years; 63% male. Median recurrent tumor volume was 3.0 cm³ (IQR, 0.8-8.7). Median single fraction SRS dose was 16 Gy (IQR, 14-19). Radiation necrosis and neurological deficits occurred in 5.5% and 8.2%, respectively. Median PRS, OS, and PFS were 12.3, 24.2, and 10.4-months. Higher SRS dose independently predicted longer PRS (HR 0.81/Gy; 95% CI 0.73-0.90, p<0.001). Dose escalation >19 Gy improved PRS (18.6 vs 11.3-months; p=0.002) without increased toxicity in PSM cohorts. MGMT methylation and unifocal recurrence were favorable prognostic factors. In the RPA, tumor volume was the primary prognostic factor; dose intensification benefited mainly patients with smaller tumors, while preserved performance status reduced risk in larger tumors. Kaplan-Meier curves confirmed clinically meaningful PRS stratification (p<0.001). CONCLUSIONS: SRS is safe and effective for select patients with first-recurrence GB. Higher prescription doses were associated with improved post-recurrence survival without added toxicity within the dose range and volumes studied with a substantial number of patients receiving bevacizumab within 30 days of SRS. Dose-intensified SRS may be considered in carefully selected patients with limited-volume recurrence and preserved performance status.

papers.abstract_full: UNLABELLED: Current understanding of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) has been shaped by phenotype-first studies in predominantly European ancestry cohorts, leaving population-level prevalence and penetrance in a multiancestry population incompletely defined. Using a genotype-first design, we analyzed whole-genome sequencing and clinical data from 374,973 unrelated All of Us participants (42.0% non-European ancestry). We identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in 10 established MODY genes and assessed carrier prevalence, diabetes penetrance, and age-dependent diabetes risk, including comparisons with noncarriers stratified by type 2 diabetes polygenic risk score (T2D PRS) and associations between T2D PRS and diabetes risk among carriers. We identified 370 carriers (0.099%; 1 in 1,013), with similar prevalence among European and African ancestry participants (0.105% in both). Diabetes penetrance was incomplete (13.4% by age 40; 43.5% by age 60) and varied by etiology: highest for GCK (56.0% by age 60), intermediate for HNF genes (HNF1A, HNF1B, and HNF4A; 45.4%), and lowest for non-GCK/HNF genes (ABCC8, INS, KCNJ11, NEUROD1, PDX1, and RFX6; 29.0%). In Cox models, carriers of variants in non-GCK/HNF genes had modestly increased diabetes risk (hazard ratio [HR] 1.64; 95% CI 1.19-2.27), which was numerically lower than among noncarriers in the top 10% of T2D PRS (HR 1.91; 95% CI 1.87-1.95). Higher T2D PRS was also associated with greater diabetes risk among carriers (HR per SD 1.32; 95% CI 1.13-1.56). These findings support equitable consideration of MODY genetic testing across ancestries and highlight substantial heterogeneity in diabetes risk among carriers of pathogenic variants in MODY genes. ARTICLE HIGHLIGHTS: Understanding of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) has been shaped by phenotype-first, predominantly European ancestry studies. We asked what the prevalence and penetrance of pathogenic MODY variants were in 374,973 unrelated All of Us participants from multiple ancestry groups and whether type 2 diabetes polygenic risk modified diabetes risk. Variants were present in 1 in 1,013, with similar prevalence in European and African ancestry individuals; penetrance varied by etiology, with diabetes risk among some carriers overlapping that of noncarriers with high polygenic risk. Higher polygenic risk was associated with greater risk among carriers. Findings support equitable consideration of MODY testing across ancestries and highlight variation in diabetes risk among carriers.

papers.abstract_full: Background:  Maternal body mass index (BMI) ≥30kg/m2 has previously been associated with reduced infant neurocognitive development, including educational attainment. The mechanistic pathway underlying this association is unclear. Objective: We examined the relationship between observed maternal BMI, maternal genetic liability for BMI, and infant mid-childhood educational attainment. We aimed to limit residual confounding by environmental factors, for example socioeconomic status. Methods: A BMI polygenic risk score (PRSBMI) was applied to eligible participants in the Pregnancy Outcome Prediction study (n=2437). Six educational outcomes through mid-childhood (age 5, age 6, and 4 domains at age 7) were regressed on (i) maternal pre-pregnancy BMI based on self-reported weight (ii) maternal PRSBMI and (iii) residual BMI unexplained by PRSBMI. Participants were stratified into four risk groups by PRSBMI risk and observed BMI. Relationships between each risk group and educational outcomes were examined. All association analyses were adjusted for confounders including school funding type, socioeconomic status, and serious childhood morbidity. Causality was evaluated using two-sample Mendelian randomisation (MR). False discovery rate (FDR) was controlled using the Benjamini-Hochsberg correction at alpha=0.05. Findings: Inverse associations were present between all education outcomes and maternal pre-pregnancy BMI, maternal PRSBMI, and maternal residual BMI. Children whose mothers had both pre-pregnancy BMI >25kg/m2 and PRSBMI z-score >0 were consistently less likely to meet educational standards compared to other risk groups. In two-sample MR an inverse relationship between maternal BMI and educational attainment was statistically significant for educational attainment aged 6, but not at ages 5 or 7 after FDR correction. Interpretation: Increased maternal pre-pregnancy BMI shows both genetic and environmental associations with reduced childhood educational attainment, although the two pathways are unlikely to be discrete. Infants of women with co-occurring high observed BMI and high genetic liability to BMI may be at highest risk of poor educational attainment.

papers.abstract_full: Autism is diagnosed more often in males than in females, but it remains unclear to what extent this reflects sex differences in autistic traits themselves or in how those traits are recognised. We compare up to four raters of the same participants, testing whether autistic trait scores differ by sex across raters, and whether the association with autism polygenic scores (PGS) differs by sex (genetic sex amplification) or rater.  We derived autistic trait scores from mother- (  n = 4,541), father- (  n = 3,674), teacher- (  n = 2,939), and self-reports (  n = 2,632) on an autism subscale of the Achenbach System of Empirically Based Assessment (ASEBA) for 12–14-year-olds in the Young Netherlands Twin Register (total  n = 6,163). Ordinal mixed-effects regression modelled a three-way interaction between PGS, rater, and sex. Measurement invariance analysis tested the subscale items for sex bias.  Mothers, fathers, and teachers rated males higher than females (odds ratios (  OR ) = 1.56, 1.49, and 2.34), whereas females rated themselves higher than males did (  OR = 0.71, males as reference). Autism PGS were associated with higher autistic trait scores (  OR = 1.22), but this association did not differ by rater or sex. One item (  "Acts too young for his/her age" ) was biased towards males in mother- and self-ratings.  These rater effects are consistent with under-recognition of autistic traits in females by external raters. In contrast, the PGS association did not differ by sex or rater, providing no evidence for sex amplification, though current autism PGS have limited predictive power.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract  Background  Social isolation and loneliness are increasingly recognized as potentially modifiable determinants of neurological health in middle-aged and older adults, but whether their associations vary according to polygenic susceptibility remains unclear. Methods  This prospective cohort included 370,475 UK Biobank participants. Cox models evaluated associations of social isolation and loneliness with five neurological disorders, including subgroup and interaction analyses. Disease-specific polygenic risk score (PRS) analyses assessed gene-by-social interaction. Results  During a median follow-up of 13.7 years, social isolation was associated with dementia (HR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.16–1.28), multiple sclerosis (MS; HR, 1.43; 95% CI, 1.14–1.78), Parkinson’s disease (PD; HR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.02–1.36), and stroke (HR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.06–1.20). Loneliness was associated with dementia (HR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.32–1.48), PD (HR, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.09–1.53), and stroke (HR, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.15–1.32). Neither exposure was associated with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and loneliness was not associated with MS. For dementia, the largest subgroup estimates were observed among never drinkers for social isolation (HR, 1.59) and non-White participants for loneliness (HR, 1.71). Concurrent social isolation and loneliness were associated with the highest hazards of dementia (HR, 1.60) and stroke (HR, 1.36), without significant multiplicative interaction between the exposures. No significant multiplicative interactions were detected between either social exposure and disease-specific PRSs. An exploratory positive HR-based RERI was observed only for social isolation and MS PRS (2.48; 95% CI, 0.17–4.68). Conclusion  Social isolation and loneliness showed distinct associations with neurological disorders. Concurrent exposure identified higher-risk groups without evidence of synergy. These observational findings support social connection as a population-health risk marker but do not establish causality or intervention effects.

papers.abstract_full: Background  Variability in low-density lipoprotein (LDL-C) response to popular diets is well documented, but the factors contributing to this variability remain unclear. We examined whether genetic predisposition to high LDL-C impacts the effects of healthy low-carbohydrate (HLC) and healthy low-fat (HLF) diets on LDL-C. Methods  The Diet Intervention Examining the Factors Interacting with Treatment Success (DIETFITS) trial randomized 609 adults (ages 18-50 years; body mass index 28-40 kg/m  2 ; not on lipid-lowering therapy) to a HLC or HLF diet for 12 months. This secondary analysis included 431 genotyped participants (HLC, n=223; HLF, n=208) with 24-hour recall and LDL-C data at baseline and 6 months. The primary exposure was a genome-wide polygenic score for LDL-C (PGS  LDL ). The outcomes were 6-month change in LDL-C, LDL-C increase versus decrease, and new-onset hypercholesterolemia (LDL-C ≥130 mg/dL). papers.abstract: Background  Hypertension is a major modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet the relative contributions of proteomic (ProtS), metabolomic (MetS), and polygenic risk scores (PRS) to incident hypertension risk remain incompletely characterized. papers.abstract_full: Background  Hypertension is a major modifiable risk factor for cardiovascular disease, yet the relative contributions of proteomic (ProtS), metabolomic (MetS), and polygenic risk scores (PRS) to incident hypertension risk remain incompletely characterized. Methods  We developed ProtS and MetS for systolic (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and hypertension using Elastic Net regression in the Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA). We incorporated these scores with previously developed BP PRSs into 5 incremental XGBoost models, with external validation in the Jackson Heart Study (JHS). We further applied transfer learning to adapt the MESA-derived models to JHS. Elastic Net selected proteins were prioritized using Mendelian randomization, colocalization, and functional analyses. Results  In MESA, model discrimination improved with the addition of omics scores, with the combined model achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.72 compared with 0.63 for the clinical baseline model. In JHS, ProtS showed the highest AUC of 0.68 and the smallest cross-cohort performance decline, compared to MetS and PRS. Incorporating measured SBP and DBP substantially improved discrimination, with the PRS+BP model achieving an AUC of 0.80 in MESA and the baseline+BP model achieving an AUC of 0.74 in JHS. Among JHS participants with normal baseline BP, ProtS provided the strongest discrimination among models without measured BP (AUC = 0.62), while PRS+BP model achieved an AUC of 0.69. Leaf-weight refreshing consistently improved calibration in JHS while preserving discrimination. Mendelian randomization identified 77 proteins associated with BP traits or hypertension, involved in vascular, inflammatory, renal, and natriuretic pathways. Conclusions  ProtS demonstrated superior predictive performance and cross-cohort transferability among the omics modalities evaluated, while measured BP remained the strongest predictors of incident hypertension. Proteomic and genetic information may provide complementary biological signals for identifying individuals at elevated hypertension risk, particularly before clinically elevated BP is detectable.

papers.abstract_full: Background  Endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), and uterine fibroids are linked to psychiatric morbidity, but evidence on causality across the full psychiatric spectrum remains limited. Methods  We assessed associations between endometriosis, PCOS, uterine fibroids and adult- onset psychiatric conditions (schizophrenia and other psychotic disorders, mood disorders, anxiety and stress-related disorders) in UK Biobank female participants using three complementary approaches: a matched-pair cohort design, a polygenic risk score (PRS)-based cohort analysis, and bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomization (MR). Sensitivity analyses were performed to test robustness. Results  Endometriosis was associated with mood disorders (OR= 1.51, 95% CI 1.40, 1.63), anxiety and stress-related disorders (OR=1.49, 95% CI 1.38, 1.62), and behavioral syndromes with physical components (OR= 1.28, 95% CI 1.01, 1.62). Uterine fibroids were associated with mood disorders (OR=1.17; 95% CI 1.11, 1.23), anxiety and stress-related disorders (OR=1.40, 95% CI 1.34, 1.48), and behavioral syndromes (OR=1.29, 95% CI 1.12, 1.48). PCOS was associated with mood disorders (OR=1.47, 95% CI 1.32, 1.64) and anxiety and stress-related disorders (OR=1.79, 95% CI 1.62,1.99), but not behavioral syndromes. No gynecologic disorder was associated with schizophrenia or other psychotic disorders. Genetic analyses supported shared liability and causal effects between fibroids and anxiety disorders. Conclusions  Women with gynecologic disorders are at increased risk of mood and anxiety- and stress-related disorders, and those with endometriosis or fibroids also face additional risk of behavioral syndromes. At least some of these risks appear driven by genetic liability, supporting routine mental health screening in gynecologic care and integrated treatment of gynecologic and mental health. Key Messages  Women with endometriosis, polycystic ovary syndrome, or uterine fibroids have 17–80% higher risks of mood and anxiety/stress-related disorders but not psychotic disorders. Genetic analyses support shared genetic liability between uterine fibroids and psychiatric disorders, with evidence for a causal effect of fibroids on anxiety disorders. These findings support integrating routine mental health screening into gynecologic care for affected women.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Stroke is a major cerebrovascular disease, and aging is a major risk factor associated with poorer outcomes. Identifying genetic mechanisms linking aging-related processes to stroke may help prioritize relevant genes and pathways. AIMS: To identify aging-related genes associated with stroke risk and explore their molecular and cellular context. STUDY DESIGN: An integrated analysis combining eQTL-based Mendelian randomization and single-cell transcriptomics. METHODS: eQTL data were obtained from eQTLGen, with stroke GWAS data from FinnGen as the discovery dataset and the GWAS Catalog as the validation dataset. MR, sensitivity, and colocalization analyses were used to evaluate associations between genetically predicted gene expression and stroke risk. Single-cell data (GSE174574) were analyzed using Seurat to characterize cell-type-specific expression of prioritized genes. GSEA and GSVA were used for pathway analysis, while RcisTarget, miRWalk, and DGIdb were used to explore regulatory and drug-gene interactions. RESULTS: In 340,999 participants, 22 aging-related genes showed nominal MR associations with stroke risk. Validation in 1,039,382 participants identified LPAR3, MEOX1, VEGFA, and PRKDC. Higher genetically predicted MEOX1 and VEGFA expression was associated with lower stroke risk, whereas LPAR3 and PRKDC were associated with higher risk. VEGFA showed additional support from regional colocalization analysis, whereas LPAR3 and MEOX1 were primarily supported by MR evidence. Regulatory analysis identified 51 predicted miRNAs and 53 drug-gene interaction records involving VEGFA and LPAR3. CONCLUSION: LPAR3, MEOX1, VEGFA, and PRKDC were prioritized as aging-related genes associated with stroke risk. VEGFA showed additional support from regional colocalization analysis, while LPAR3, MEOX1, and PRKDC require further functional validation.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: The peripapillary retinal nerve fibre layer (pRNFL) thickness and Bruch's membrane opening-minimum rim width (BMO-MRW) are structural biomarkers for glaucoma. We conducted large-scale multi-cohort genome-wide association meta-analyses of global and sectoral pRNFL thickness and BMO-MRW to disentangle their genetic architecture. METHODS: We included up to 25,942 and 12,080 participants for global and sectoral pRNFL thickness and BMO-MRW, respectively, from the International Glaucoma Genetics Consortium. Conditional analysis was used to identify loci with association evidence beyond intraocular pressure (IOP). Genes at these loci were prioritised to identify candidate causal genes using transcriptome-wide association studies and colocalisation of genetic and expression quantitative trait loci. FINDINGS: Nine loci were identified for each of global pRNFL thickness and global BMO-MRW. The analyses further revealed 20 and 11 loci for pRNFL and BMO-MRW sectors, respectively, comprising both shared and sector-specific loci. Interestingly, the effect sizes of rs1313237, a well-known optic nerve locus, had opposite effect directions between pRNFL temporal and nasal regions. Robust associations were observed for genes relevant to IOP-adjusted glaucoma biology, including NMNAT2 and TRIOBP. INTERPRETATION: Our findings highlighted the potential neurodegenerative or developmental genes identified for pRNFL thickness and BMO-MRW whose effects are not fully mediated by IOP. We also elucidated genetic differences among pRNFL sectors, which require further investigation to assess clinical relevance. papers.abstract_full: Heritability of regional subcortical brain volumes (rSBVs) quantifies the contribution of genetic variation to individual differences in subcortical brain morphology during neurodevelopment. rSBVs are highly heritable in adults but are not well characterized in adolescents. The Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development study (ABCD), collected across 21 US sites, provides data to characterize the heritability of subcortical structures in adolescence. However, in a multi-site multi-ancestry study, such as ABCD, site-specific effects may co-occur with genetic effects, which can bias heritability estimates. Existing methods that adjust for site effects require additional steps and can lead to inconsistent estimates. We propose a random-effect model-based MOM approach to estimate heritability that is a single-step asymptotically consistent estimator even when ancestries are differentially distributed across sites. Our approach performed well under a wide range of simulations. The proposed approach yielded heritability estimates similar to previous results derived from single-site studies and studies on different age groups, with the cerebellar cortex and hippocampus showing the highest estimated heritability (>50%).

papers.abstract_full: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) has substantial heritability. Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) often use single-nucleotide polygenic risk scores to estimate this inherited risk, but macro-scale structural alterations remain under-explored. We evaluated whether chromosome-level structural variation (CLSV) provides a predictive signal for AMI. We quantified this variation as statistical moments of microarray Log R Ratio (LRR) distributions across 128 segments of the genome. We performed 1:1 matching between cases and controls on sex at birth, self-reported race, and age (\(\:\le\:\pm\:2\) years) within the All of Us Research Program Controlled Tier dataset (\(\:N=3,290\)) to eliminate demographic confounding. We evaluated Random Forest models across 10 independent stratified cross-validation splits. The CLSV model achieved a 10-split mean held-out test ROC AUC of 0.529 (SD: \(\:0.048\), 10-split range: \(\:0.439\) to \(\:0.604\)). This performance is statistically indistinguishable from a scrambled target control (\(\:0.491\), 10-split range: \(\:0.465\) to \(\:0.546\)) and overlaps random chance (\(\:0.500\)). A positive biological control predicting sex at birth using the same genomic moment extraction pipeline achieved near-perfect discrimination (mean AUC = \(\:0.999\), 10-split range: \(\:0.997\) to \(\:1.000\)), confirming high technical validity. We establish with 95% statistical confidence that any true predictive signal carried by broad structural genomic variation in an unconfounded matched cohort is less than an upper 95% confidence limit of 0.585 (Nadeau-Bengio corrected, mean AUC = 0.529). Our findings suggest that macro-scale structural variation does not explain missing heritability or provide clinical risk discrimination for AMI.

papers.abstract_full: Background Vascular dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a contributor to Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet the genetic mechanisms linking blood pressure (BP) and AD remain incompletely understood. We investigated shared genetic architecture between AD and systolic blood pressure (SBP), diastolic blood pressure (DBP), and pulse pressure (PP) to identify locus-specific mechanisms connecting vascular regulation and neurodegeneration. Results We analyzed genome-wide association study summary statistics from individuals of European ancestry using global and local genetic correlation and conjunctional false discovery rate (conjFDR), followed by cis-Mendelian randomization (cis-MR), functional annotation, expression quantitative trait locus associations, and AD-specific multi-omic evidence. AD showed modest negative global genetic correlations with BP but significant local genetic correlation at eight regions. ConjFDR identified 42 high-confidence variants across 22 independent LD regions, with PRKD3 , NBEAL1 , NDUFAF6 , SPI1 , and the APOE region supported by both local genetic correlation and conjFDR. Cis-MR provided evidence for effects of BP on AD at multiple regions, with ACE and the APOE region showing significant effects for all three BP traits. Integrative analysis most strongly prioritized the APOE region, with convergent evidence at ACE and NBEAL1 and additional signals implicating immune and mitochondrial pathways. Conclusions The genetic relationship between AD and BP is characterized by heterogeneous, locus-specific overlap not fully captured by genome-wide genetic correlation. Convergent evidence implicates APOE , ACE , NBEAL1 , and other loci involved in vascular, immune, and mitochondrial biology, supporting multiple, partially BP-trait-specific mechanisms linking vascular regulation to AD.

papers.abstract_full: Cardiac remodeling underlies cardiomyopathy and heart failure, yet how common genetic effects are organized across the four chambers, and whether they influence phenotypic variability beyond additive genetic effects, remains unclear. We analyzed 22 cardiac magnetic resonance phenotypes in up to 77,271 UK Biobank participants. Additive mapping identified 748 locus-trait associations across 239 regions. Multivariate fine-mapping revealed that 96% of signals showed effects across multiple cardiac chambers, while resolving independent signals with distinct anatomical profiles, including predominantly atrial and ventricular signals at RBM20. Fine-mapped signal sharing formed three robust communities corresponding broadly to atrial function, chamber remodeling and ventricular systolic function. Variance mapping identified 19 associations, 13 without a nearby additive signal. Individual variance loci and polygenic effects generalized to clinical echocardiographic phenotypes and outcomes in the Penn Medicine Biobank. These findings reveal cardiac common-variant architecture as broadly shared yet locally heterogeneous and identify phenotypic variability as a partly distinct genetic dimension.

papers.abstract_full: To leverage independent genetic evidence from multiple species, we developed a cross-species gene-based GWAS meta-analysis framework and applied this to Dizygotic Twinning (DZT) in humans and cattle. After meta-analysis within species, we converted human and cattle GWAS summary statistics to gene-level association signals within each species, mapped genes across species through human–cattle orthology, and then combined gene-level evidence for orthologous genes across the two species. DZT is defined as giving birth to multiple offspring after a single pregnancy resulting from spontaneous multiple ovulation. In humans, DZT occurs in about 1% of pregnancies with heritability estimates of 20% to 30% whilst in cattle DZT occurs in 1-5% of pregnancies and heritability is estimated at about 11%. Here, we present the largest human GWAS meta-analysis including data from 1,395,285 participants. We identified 16 genetic regions of interest, including 12 independent loci from the SNP based analyses and 4 genes identified in the gene-based MAGMA analyses. Among the prioritized genes are follicle stimulation hormone receptor (FSHR) and growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF9), that both are involved in ovarian folliculogenesis. Cattle GWAS summary statistics were based on data from 2,656 Irish Holstein bulls with estimated breeding values for predisposition to twinning based on 2,238,936 birth records, and 86,391 German Holstein dams. After combining the gene-level analyses for 13,225 genes mapped as orthologous across the human and cattle data we identify FSHR as a central locus for DZT in both humans and cattle. We find evidence of additional associations, including ACVR2A, which plays a role in embryonic implantation and TUFM, which has previously been implicated in premature ovarian insufficiency. Our approach provides a promising framework for future cross-species comparative GWAS studies. papers.abstract_full: Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, yet biomarkers capable of identifying individuals at risk before clinical onset are lacking, and the molecular mechanisms preceding disease onset remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated plasma proteomic, metabolomic, and genomic data from the UK Biobank to characterize molecular changes preceding epilepsy and evaluate their predictive and causal relevance. We quantified 2,923 plasma proteins in ∼53,000 participants and followed incident epilepsy for up to 15 years before epilepsy diagnosis. Cox proportional hazards analyses identified 116 proteins associated with incident epilepsy, led by neurofilament light chain (NEFL; HR=2.03) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15; HR=1.73). These proteins were enriched for extracellular signaling, immune regulation, and cell-death pathways and displayed distinct subtype-and age-specific signatures. A proteomic risk score comprising 32 proteins stratified epilepsy risk, with individuals in the highest quintile exhibiting a 3.5-fold greater risk than those in the lowest quintile (AUC=0.70). In parallel, 154 of 249 circulating metabolites were associated with incident epilepsy, with the strongest inverse association observed for citrate (HR=0.72) and positive associations across HDL-related metabolites (HR=1.16–1.21), implicating dysregulated energy and lipoprotein metabolism. A metabolomic risk score showed more modest discrimination (AUC=0.63). Integrating proteomic, metabolomic, polygenic, and demographic information yielded an overall AUC of 0.71 for incident epilepsy; in a separate cross-sectional analysis of individuals with early-onset epilepsy discrimination reached an AUC of 0.79. Proteome-wide cis-pQTL Mendelian randomization identified 12 proteins associated with epilepsy after false discovery rate correction, predominantly for genetic generalized epilepsy. O-GlcNAcase (OGA), a regulator of protein O-GlcNAcylation with established roles in neuronal function and synaptic plasticity, showed the strongest protective association (OR=0.71, FDR=2.7×10⁻⁸). Serine protease 53 (PRSS53), a poorly characterized serine protease, showed strong evidence for a potential shared causal variant with epilepsy (colocalization PP.H4=0.95). Together, these findings demonstrate that circulating molecular alterations precede epilepsy diagnosis by years and reveal complementary proteomic, metabolic, and genetic determinants of disease susceptibility, providing a framework for biologically informed risk stratification and therapeutic target prioritization.

papers.abstract_full: Hybrid maize (  Zea mays L.) parents are chosen within heterotic groups. Drought and heat stress are expected to become more frequent, but little is known about how they change the additive variance of each group and where in the genome it lies. We analyzed testcross grain yield from 62 Genomes to Fields environments, classified as low or high stress by climate. For 1,362 parents from three heterotic groups and two doubled-haploid families, we fitted a genomic model with group deviations and calculated local genomic estimated breeding values in 164-kb segments. In the heterotic groups, high stress reduced additive variance by 40–57%, and the genetic correlation between conditions was 0.73–0.99. Within groups, the distribution of variance across the genome was similar between conditions (correlation 0.84–1.00), and genotype-by-environment interaction was spread over many low-variance segments. Genome-wide association detected 25 loci under low stress and 18 under high stress, none shared, but half or more lay in high-effect, high-variance segments that were nearly the same in both conditions. The best possible cross between the two heterotic pools exceeded the best evaluated hybrid by 105–117%, a gap that depended on segment size, not on stress. With 25 founders, stacking the best segments reached 94–95% of the pool potential, versus 56–92% for selection on total breeding value, whose founders were more related. Founders chosen in one condition reached, in the other, 94–100% of the potential of those chosen there. Local breeding values can guide the choice of donors and founders under both conditions.  Article summary  Hybrid maize breeders choose parents within heterotic groups, and drought and heat stress are expected to increase. Using public Genomes to Fields trials, we measured how stress changes the additive genetic variance of each group and where it lies in the genome. Stress reduced the variance in the three heterotic groups, but the regions with the most variance were nearly the same under low and high stress. Founders chosen by combining the best genome segments reached almost all of the pool’s potential and kept it under the other condition. Breeders can use segment values to choose parents across stress levels.

papers.title: LAMP sheds light on how sequence to function models learn variant effects during post-training
papers.abstract: Genomic sequence-to-function (S2F) models show promise for interpreting noncoding genetic variation, yet they currently underestimate the effects of most causal variants. papers.abstract_full: Genomic sequence-to-function (S2F) models show promise for interpreting noncoding genetic variation, yet they currently underestimate the effects of most causal variants. This leads to fine-mapping failures that are reflected in their underperformance relative to linear baselines at predicting gene expression across individuals from personal genome sequences. Improving personal genome predictions, which reflect this underestimation, is therefore critical. There is broad interest in post-training S2F models to improve these predictions, yet many groups have shown that doing so with personal genome sequences and paired expression values does not meaningfully improve predictions on held-out genes and people (HOGP). Why these post-training efforts to improve predictions on HOGP, and therefore causal variant underestimation, remains unclear. To understand why, we introduce LAMP (Learning of Artificial Motif Perturbations), a framework in which artificial SNVs (aSNVs) perturbing transcription factor motifs are substituted into personal genome datasets genome-wide with large, consistent, and causal effects on gene expression. These aSNVs are designed to be deliberately easy to learn, yet fine-tuning Enformer using this LAMP framework led to persistent underperformance on HOGP, which suggests fundamental challenges for learning variant effects during post-training that are independent of the complexity of natural genetic variation. Our findings suggest this underperformance is caused in part due to challenges learning to strengthen enhancer-gene links during post-training. In particular, models struggle with learning to rewire attention weights to relate aSNV detection, over distance, to a change in expression of the target gene. This limitation is caused by strong pre-trained priors that downweight distal regulatory elements, causing extreme data inefficiency in learning to attend to distal elements, and variants within them, during post-training. Second, sequence variability between loci containing different instances of the same TF motif obscures otherwise easy-to-learn motif perturbation patterns and also hinder learning of variant effects. Our results suggest that the scale of observed human genetic variation is vastly insufficient to maximize S2F model accuracy on HOGP via simple fine-tuning, consistent with past outcomes. We propose data augmentation strategies that, under LAMP, significantly improve learning of aSNV effects by strategically targeting the limitations we identified. We release LAMP as a tool to troubleshoot and optimize future S2F post-training objectives.

papers.abstract_full: Abstract    Bacterial wilt caused by  Ralstonia solanacearum  is a major constraint to eggplant (  Solanum melongena  L.) production, and the genetic basis of resistance remains insufficiently characterized. In this study, we investigated the inheritance and genomic basis of bacterial wilt resistance using an F₂ population of 260 individuals derived from a cross between the resistant cultivar Utkal Anushree and the susceptible line BCB 40. Phenotypic evaluation following artificial inoculation indicated that resistance was predominantly controlled by a major recessive locus. QTL-seq analysis of contrasting resistant and susceptible DNA bulks identified three candidate genomic regions on chromosome 3 (91.0-91.8 Mb) and chromosome 11 (6.7-7.0 Mb and 7.4–8.4 Mb). Screening of 110 SSR markers identified emb01D10 and em135a as polymorphic between the parents and contrasting DNA bulks. Genotyping of the F₂ population further confirmed their close association with the resistance locus, demonstrating their potential as molecular markers for bacterial wilt resistance. Comparative sequence analysis of the candidate regions identified several SNPs and InDel polymorphisms, providing additional sequence variation for fine mapping and candidate gene identification. Collectively, these results define genomic regions associated with bacterial wilt resistance and identify closely linked molecular markers in eggplant. The genomic resources generated in this study provide a basis for further molecular dissection of resistance and facilitate marker-assisted selection for bacterial wilt resistance breeding.

papers.title: Perturbation-induced gene programs map the hidden regulatory architecture of complex diseases.
papers.abstract: Steady-state molecular profiles incompletely capture the regulatory programs through which genetic variation influences complex disease, particularly programs that emerge only when cells are perturbed. Here, we introduce Perturbscape, a computational framework that learns multiscale gene programs for individual perturbations in a CRISPR Perturb-seq screen using linear and nonlinear contrastive approaches alongside complementary program-learning methods, and integrates them with human genetics to…
papers.abstract_full: Steady-state molecular profiles incompletely capture the regulatory programs through which genetic variation influences complex disease, particularly programs that emerge only when cells are perturbed. Here, we introduce Perturbscape, a computational framework that learns multiscale gene programs for individual perturbations in a CRISPR Perturb-seq screen using linear and nonlinear contrastive approaches alongside complementary program-learning methods, and integrates them with human genetics to prioritize disease-relevant genes, perturbations and downstream regulatory pathways. Across 15,859 perturbation-by-context profiles from 7 Perturb-seq systems and 53 complex diseases and traits (mean GWAS N=291K), perturbation-induced programs showed up to 4.3-fold higher heritability informativeness than analogous steady-state multi-tissue gene prioritization, and retained significant conditional heritability informativeness across all 34 matched cell system-trait comparisons after accounting for steady-state prioritization. Preserving perturbation-specific programs further yielded 2.5-5.3-fold higher trait relevance scores than programs derived from control cells, pooled perturbations or differential-expression summaries. In K562, Perturbscape-prioritized genes showed stronger enrichment for rare-variant burden genes than steady-state prioritization and were supported by orthogonal enhancer CRISPRi screens. In HepG2, LDL cholesterol-associated perturbation- induced programs specifically revealed statin-responsive pathways not significantly enriched by steady-state PoPS prioritization, supported by pharmacological transcriptional responses and population plasma proteomics. Perturbscape also recovered blood-related trait-conditioned trans-regulatory relationships that were specifically supported by population trans-eQTLs in IFN-γ-stimulated monocytes (OR = 1.30, P=1.6e-05). Perturbscape further revealed developmental-stage-specific convergence between monogenic diabetes regulators and polygenic T2D risk during pancreatic islet differentiation, and neuronal-subclass-specific autism-associated regulatory programs in vivo . Together, these findings establish perturbation-induced gene programs as a complementary layer of disease-relevant regulatory information, revealing genetically informative pathways and context-specific regulatory relationships incompletely represented by steady-state molecular atlases.

papers.title: Gene Burden Testing for Rare and Genetic Disease Studies: A Practical Beginner-Oriented Workflow.
papers.abstract: Gene burden testing is a practical analytic framework for evaluating whether multiple rare variants within a gene, transcript, or biologically defined variant set are collectively associated with disease. This strategy is especially useful in rare disease and sequencing-based genetic studies because most individual rare variants are too uncommon to achieve adequate statistical power on their own, whereas aggregating them into a biologically meaningful set can increase the ability to detect assoc…
papers.abstract_full: Gene burden testing is a practical analytic framework for evaluating whether multiple rare variants within a gene, transcript, or biologically defined variant set are collectively associated with disease. This strategy is especially useful in rare disease and sequencing-based genetic studies because most individual rare variants are too uncommon to achieve adequate statistical power on their own, whereas aggregating them into a biologically meaningful set can increase the ability to detect association. This chapter is written as a general bioinformatics method rather than as a disease-specific protocol, so that it can be applied to Mendelian disorders, complex diseases enriched for rare coding alleles, unresolved exome cases, and candidate genes prioritized from wet-lab experiments. The workflow covers study design, data preparation, sample and variant quality control, variant annotation, definition of qualifying variants, selection of burden and kernel-based tests, covariate adjustment, and interpretation of positive and negative findings. Emphasis is placed on methods that are accessible to graduate students and physician-scientists using public or institutional sequencing datasets, and on practical decisions that strongly influence reproducibility, such as ancestry matching, allele-frequency thresholds, phenotype handling, and sensitivity analyses. The chapter also positions gene burden testing within the broader landscape of modern statistical genetics, including collapsing methods, weighted burden tests, variance-component methods, and extensions toward oligogenic or digenic disease architectures.

papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have limited power to detect rare-variant associations. The sequence kernel association test (SKAT) enhances power by jointly testing variants within a region, but its power depends on how the kernel represents genetic similarity. papers.abstract_full: Genome-wide association studies have limited power to detect rare-variant associations. The sequence kernel association test (SKAT) enhances power by jointly testing variants within a region, but its power depends on how the kernel represents genetic similarity. The weighted-linear kernel predominates in rare-variant testing, whereas the weighted Gaussian kernel remains less widely used. Varying the Gaussian bandwidth hyperparameter changes the representation of genetic similarity from localized and nonlinear to increasingly linear-like. However, very small hyperparameter values can cause similarities between nonidentical weighted genotype profiles to collapse toward zero, whereas very large values cause the weighted Gaussian kernel to behave increasingly like weighted-linear SKAT and therefore provide little distinct information. Because the underlying genetic architecture is unknown, no single hyperparameter value can be expected to work best across regions. We propose GausSKAT, which evaluates weighted Gaussian SKAT over a phenotype-independent, data-adaptive hyperparameter grid and combines the resulting dependent p  values using the aggregated Cauchy association test (ACAT). The grid endpoints are informed by weighted genetic distances and the large-hyperparameter behavior of the covariate-adjusted kernel. In simulations, GausSKAT generally achieved higher power than weighted-linear and weighted identity-by-state SKAT under the genetic architectures considered. The best-performing hyperparameter value varied across settings, supporting aggregation across multiple values. In the Dallas Heart Study analysis of triglyceride levels, the relative performance of GausSKAT and weighted-linear SKAT varied among ANGPTL gene-family variant sets. These findings support GausSKAT as a complementary extension that broadens the similarity structures represented within SKAT.

papers.abstract: In contrast to large-effect monogenic variants, which are highly penetrant regardless of genetic background, variants with more modest effect sizes depend on a carrier's genetic background to manifest disease. papers.abstract_full: In contrast to large-effect monogenic variants, which are highly penetrant regardless of genetic background, variants with more modest effect sizes depend on a carrier's genetic background to manifest disease. For many complex traits, including idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), polygenic risk scores (PRS) have been shown to capture a significant proportion of the genetic background risk. While a rare-variant association test incorporating a PRS covariate to account for the genetic background has been demonstrated to improve statistical power for gene discovery in quantitative traits, for binary traits, this approach shows limited or no power gain over PRS-unadjusted tests. Here, we propose a novel rare-variant association test for binary traits that jointly models the contribution of rare variants and PRS under a liability threshold model. In simulated datasets, our new method, liability threshold burden test (LTBT), shows a well-controlled false positive rate and outperforms the sensitivity of existing methods. To demonstrate this new method, we apply it to sequencing datasets for IPF, a rare but highly morbid lung disease. By accounting for an individual's genetic background with PRS, we identify and formally replicate a significant novel association of rare predicted damaging missense variants in HTRA3 (HtrA serine peptidase 3) with IPF.

papers.abstract_full: Genetic studies of chronic disease typically collapse longitudinal clinical histories into binary case-control outcomes, obscuring disease timing and differences in genetic association patterns across disease transitions. Time-to-event analysis can preserve this information, but rare-variant analysis of post-diagnosis progression is challenged by sparse carrier-events and extensive censoring. We developed GATE-GENE, a scalable gene-based framework that maintains calibration under these conditions. Across 300 onset phenotypes in UK Biobank (UKB), GATE-GENE identified 107 exome-wide significant germline associations involving 89 genes and 67 diseases. Across 95 multi-state trajectories comprising baseline (T0), an upstream disease state (T1) and a downstream disease state (T2), disease onset (T0→T1) and subsequent progression (T1→T2) showed limited detectable sharing of rare-variant association signals. Progression showed greater concordance of gene-level association signals with downstream phenotypes (T0→T2) when the analyses shared T2 events occurring after T1. Removing overlapping downstream events reduced the median correlation between gene-level association signals from 0.063 to 0.001, after accounting for background correlation. Null simulations reproduced the relationship between event overlap and concordance without genetic effects, whereas additional simulations showed that near-zero concordance could persist despite extensive underlying causal-gene sharing. This attenuation was reproduced across three ancestry groups in All of Us. Cross-biobank meta-analysis identified 12 additional exome-wide significant progression associations beyond three UKB discoveries, although clinical sensitivity analyses suggested that the strongest  PKD1 signals largely reflected underlying cystic kidney disease. Together, these findings establish GATE-GENE for investigating rare-variant associations with disease timing and progression, while demonstrating how overlapping clinical events and limited carrier-event information complicate inference about genetic sharing across disease transitions.

papers.title: Exploring Collaborative Approaches: An Analysis of Plastic and Cardiothoracic Surgery Integration.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Median sternotomy remains a standard approach for thoracic access, but optimal closure techniques, particularly in high-risk patients, remain undefined. Although wire cerclage remains the predominant method, sternal rigid plate fixation (SRPF) offers advantages in select populations. This study examines current US practice patterns and collaboration between cardiothoracic (CT) and plastic and reconstructive surgery (PRS) teams regarding SRPF. METHODS: A 19-question cross-sectional survey was distributed to 550 US CT surgeons; 40 attending surgeons responded. The survey assessed closure methods, risk stratification, and interdisciplinary collaboration. RESULTS: Most respondents routinely used wire cerclage, with only one reporting routine use of SRPF for primary closure. Although 37 surgeons had access to PRS, few involved PRS in primary or secondary closure, and CT teams generally managed complications such as dehiscence or nonunion independently. Risk stratification varied widely, and few surgeons considered any comorbidity an absolute indication for SRPF. Only 1 respondent reported a formal consulting relationship with a device manufacturer, suggesting minimal industry influence. Given the low response rate, findings should be considered exploratory. CONCLUSIONS: Practice patterns for sternal closure vary considerably, with limited interdisciplinary collaboration despite evidence supporting SRPF in high-risk patients. Standardized decision-making tools and enhanced CT training may facilitate evidence-based adoption of SRPF and improve outcomes in complex sternal wound management.

papers.abstract_full: BACKGROUND: Cancer screening programmes apply uniform criteria irrespective of inherited risk. Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) have been proposed as a promising tool to stratify individual cancer risk and tailor screening strategies. However, whether PRS-informed strategies improve health outcomes compared with current practices remains uncertain. We aimed to synthesise the available evidence on the projected clinical utility of PRS-stratified cancer screening across six malignancies. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science from inception to March 15, 2026, for studies evaluating PRS-stratified screening for breast, colorectal, prostate, lung, gastric, or cervical cancer. Eligible outcomes included cancer-specific mortality, life-years gained (LYG), quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), overdiagnosis, and false-positive rates. Risk of bias was assessed using the ISPOR-AMCP-NPC questionnaire for modelling studies and ROBINS-I for observational studies. Certainty of evidence was appraised using the GRADE framework. FINDINGS: Of 20,Simulated 100 million 058 records identified, 25 studies were included (22 decision-analytic modelling studies, 3 observational studies) covering five malignancies; no eligible studies were identified for cervical cancer. Modelled PRS-stratified strategies were projected to improve QALYs for breast, colorectal, gastric, and lung cancer, whereas results for prostate cancer were heterogeneous. Modelled mortality reductions were projected for colorectal, gastric, and lung cancer, although evidence for the latter two rested on single studies. For breast cancer, modelled mortality outcomes were inconsistent and dependent on comparator intensity. For prostate cancer, modelling studies primarily projected reductions in overdiagnosis rather than mortality improvement. Across all cancer sites, the absolute magnitude of incremental benefit over non-stratified screening was modest. Harms increased in high-risk groups receiving intensified surveillance. The certainty of evidence was rated very low for all outcomes across all cancer types, driven by serious risk of bias and very serious indirectness, reflecting limited transferability across populations and healthcare systems. INTERPRETATION: PRS-stratified screening shows consistent but modest potential to improve the efficiency of cancer screening, particularly for breast, colorectal, and prostate cancer, although the certainty of evidence remains very low. PRS-stratified screening should remain investigational pending validation through prospective trials powered for clinical endpoints, conducted in ancestrally diverse populations, and incorporating equity-sensitive implementation frameworks. FUNDING: This study was funded by the European Union under Grant Agreement No. 101183265 (Joint Action JANE-2).

papers.abstract_full: PURPOSE: To evaluate the impact of initial recurrence and metastatic sites on survival outcomes in gastric cancer patients after radical gastrectomy. METHODS: A retrospective study was conducted on 1,140 patients with pathologically confirmed gastric cancer who underwent radical gastrectomy between September 2016 and December 2023. Patients were categorized into six groups according to initial recurrence and recurrence site: no recurrence, local recurrence, liver metastasis, peritoneal/retroperitoneal metastasis, multiple-site peritoneal metastasis, and other sites. Overall survival (OS) and Post-Recurrence Survival (PRS) were analyzed using Kaplan-Meier and log-ran k tests. Independent prognostic factors were identified by Cox regression. RESULTS: Age ≥60 years, CEA ≥5U/ml, pathological type (other), T4 Stage, perineural invasion and lymphovascular invasion were independent risk factors for poor OS, while middle-third and lower-third gastric location were protective factors. As for DFS, tumor differentiation, lymph node metastasis, perineural invasion, and site of recurrence/metastasis were significantly associated with the PRS. In the multivariable analysis, only perineural invasion remained an independent risk factor for PRS (HR = 1.588, P= 0.005). Among 222 patients with recurrence, patients with Multiple-site peritoneal metastasis had the numerically shortest median OS (20 months, 95%CI 17.040-22.960) among the five recurrence subgroups. No statistically significant between-group differences were identified after Bonferroni correction for 10 pairwise log-rank comparisons. PRS was longest in liver metastasis patients (10 months), significantly longer than multiple-site peritoneal metastasis (3 months, P < 0.001), and patients with peritoneal/retroperitoneal metastasis had longer PRS than those with multiple-site peritoneal metastases (5 vs. 3 months, P = 0.028). Comprehensive therapy was associated with significantly longer PRS compared with supportive care (9 vs. 3 months, P < 0.001) and chemotherapy alone (9 vs. 4 months, P = 0.002). CONCLUSION: PRS differed among patients with different initial recurrence/metastatic patterns. However, the initial recurrence/metastatic site was not independently associated with PRS. Perineural invasion was independently associated with shorter PRS and OS and may serve as a reference factor for post-recurrence prognostic assessment. Patients receiving comprehensive therapy after recurrence showed longer PRS.

papers.abstract_full: Social anxiety disorder (SAD) is a common psychiatric condition characterized by a consistent fear of social evaluation. Despite heritability estimates of up to 69%, genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of SAD remain limited relative to other psychiatric disorders. Furthermore, the contribution of environmental factors, particularly rural versus urban residence, to SAD risk is poorly characterized. Using the All of Us dataset (N=414,830, Ncases=10,918), our aims were to: (1) identify genetic risk loci for SAD through within-ancestry GWAS (N=1,467-222,500), cross-ancestry meta-analysis, and a European-ancestry meta-analysis (N =788,384); (2) further characterize the genetic architecture of SAD through polygenic risk score (PRS), phenome-wide association (PheWAS), laboratory-wide association (LabWAS), and genetic correlation; and (3) stratify all analyses by rural and urban environment. Across all ancestries examined, rural residence was associated with increased odds of SAD (OR=1.42, 95%; CI (1.36-1.50); p<5×10 -8 ). Although no genome-wide significant loci were identified, several loci reached suggestive significance, notably an intronic variant in NEGR1 (rs12065683), a gene with prior associations to anxiety and neurodevelopmental disorders. PheWAS analyses identified ear disorders as the most nominally significant phenotype (p=3.76x10 -5 ; OR=1.45) and significant associations with lymphocyte count were identified in the LabWAS (p=1.80x10 -5 ). These findings provide further insight into the genetic architecture of SAD and suggest that residential environment may modify risk. Larger-scale genetic studies will be required to validate the observed suggestive loci and gene x environment interaction models to form conclusions regarding the true effect of residence.

papers.abstract_full: Biological sex influences the prevalence and progression of several brain disorders, yet it remains unclear whether genetic risk interacts with sex in relation to case-control status or brain health. Using data from up to 220 836 females and 187 651 males in the UK Biobank (aged 39-81), we assessed how sex and polygenic risk scores (PRSs) for major depressive disorder (PRSMDD), Alzheimer's disease (PRSAD), schizophrenia (PRSSCZ), and Parkinson's disease (PRSPD) relate to case-control status and MRI-derived brain age gap (BAG) as a proxy of brain health. We tested for sex differences in PRSs and performed regression analyses examining associations between sex, PRSs, and both outcomes. We then compared models with sex-pooled or sex-specific PRSs to explore whether sex-specific PRSs improve predictive accuracy. PRSSCZ was higher in females, while no other PRSs differed by sex. A significant PRSAD-by-sex interaction revealed weaker associations with AD case-control status in males than females. Sex-pooled models outperformed sex-specific models for case-control status, apart from PRSAD, where the female-only PRSAD model outperformed the sex-pooled model. No sex-by-PRS interactions were significantly associated with BAG. However, male sex, higher PRSMDD, higher PRSAD, and lower PRSPD were associated with higher BAG, indicative of an older brain age. BAG model performance did not differ between sex-pooled and sex-specific PRS models. In summary, while sex-specific PRSs currently offer limited value over sex-pooled scores, the superior performance of the female-specific PRSAD model suggests that the value of sex-specific PRSs will likely grow with increased statistical power. Link to preregistration and preprint: https://osf.io/a8pt2/ .

papers.abstract: A combination of genetic and environmental factors working in interplay is thought to underlie differences in symptoms of psychopathology between adolescents. Yet, studies that have investigated gene-environment interaction in isolated aspects of developmental psychopathology lack robust effects, highlighting the need for a broader approach. We adopted a multivariable framework to investigate gene-environment interaction in internalising and externalising symptoms of psychopathology in a sample …
papers.abstract_full: A combination of genetic and environmental factors working in interplay is thought to underlie differences in symptoms of psychopathology between adolescents. Yet, studies that have investigated gene-environment interaction in isolated aspects of developmental psychopathology lack robust effects, highlighting the need for a broader approach. We adopted a multivariable framework to investigate gene-environment interaction in internalising and externalising symptoms of psychopathology in a sample of 3337 16-year-olds from the Twins Early Development Study. We used penalised regression models to examine the main effects of genetic factors (G), indexed by combining 13 polygenic scores for psychopathology, and environmental factors (E), measured by combining multiple environmental exposures during childhood and adolescence, on symptoms of psychopathology. We also examined their additive effects (G+E) and their interaction (G×E). Polygenic scores accounted for, on average, 2.7% of the variance in symptoms of psychopathology, with stronger predictions for externalising symptoms, while environmental measures alone accounted for an average of 7.1% of the variance. G+E accounted for an average of 9.1% of differences between adolescents in symptoms of psychopathology. We observed small G×E effects for internalising symptoms, accounting for an average of 1.1% of the variance. Children with a higher genetic risk showed higher levels of internalising symptoms, especially when exposed to more chaos at home and harsher parenting. Our findings indicate that genetic and environmental influences contribute additively, underscoring the importance of jointly considering both factors to enhance our understanding of youth psychopathology. At the same time, our results highlight the persistent challenges involved in identifying robust G×E effects.

papers.abstract_full: Ensemble learning has become a cornerstone for im proving the predictive accuracy of polygenic risk scores (PRSs), and nearly all recent multi-ancestry PRS methods incorporate ensemble learning as a final step. However, existing ensemble approaches require individual-level genotype data for model training, limiting their real-world applications, especially in non-European populations with insufficient genomic samples. Here we introduce a statistical framework for constructing regularized ensemble PRS that integrates a large number of candidate PRS models using only genome-wide association study summary statistics. Through extensive analyses across multiple traits and populations, we demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art PRS approaches within and across ancestries. This framework enables seamless integration of newly developed PRS models with existing ones, providing a scalable and general solution for future PRS development and application.
